# Face Culling and Visibility Optimization

Also called: Interior Polygon Removal, Removing Interior Polygons

## Overview
Face Culling and Visibility Optimization is a family of techniques used in [blocky meshing](#31-blocky-meshing.md) to reduce the geometric complexity of voxel terrain by eliminating faces that are occluded by adjacent solid blocks or invisible to the camera [S1, unofficial]. It solves the performance bottleneck of naively rendering all six faces of every [voxel cube](#4076-voxel-data-layout.md), which results in excessive triangle counts and GPU fill-rate waste [S2, unofficial]. What sets this family apart from its siblings is its focus on pre-rasterization optimization: it operates during the [mesh construction](#1022-isosurface-point-indexing-and-mesh-assembly.md) phase to minimize the vertex and index buffer size sent to the GPU, rather than relying on runtime rasterization culling or post-processing [S1, unofficial].

## Shared principles
All methods in this family share the core principle of reducing the number of rendered primitives by identifying and discarding geometry that does not contribute to the final image. The fundamental mechanism involves checking the occupancy or visibility state of neighboring voxels or camera viewpoints to determine if a face should be generated.

### Neighbor-Based Culling
The most common approach is neighbor-based culling. For a voxel at position $P$ with a face normal $N$, the method checks the voxel at $P_{neighbor} = P + N$. If $P_{neighbor}$ is occupied by a solid block, the face at $P$ in direction $N$ is internal and is culled [S1, unofficial]. If $P_{neighbor}$ is empty (air) or out of bounds, the face is potentially visible and is added to the mesh [S2, unofficial].

### View-Dependent Culling
Some methods extend neighbor checks with view-dependent tests. This involves determining the orientation of a face relative to the camera view direction. If a face is back-facing (the dot product of the face normal and the view direction is positive, indicating it faces away from the camera), it is culled [S1, unofficial]. This is often combined with [internal face masking](#4569-voxel-backface-culling-and-internal-face-masking.md) to reject shared faces between neighboring voxels [S1, unofficial].

### Multi-View Consistency
For non-voxelized or complex meshes, visibility is determined by projecting vertices into multiple camera views and comparing their depths against reference depth maps or binary masks. A vertex or face is retained only if it is consistently visible across a threshold number of views [S1, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Voxel Block Placement with Face Culling](923-voxel-block-placement-with-face-culling.md)
A technique for dynamically updating a voxel chunk's internal state and face visibility when blocks are placed or removed, using neighbor checks to toggle shared faces without regenerating the entire mesh. It differs from its sibling [Greedy face merging](8935-greedy-face-merging.md) by maintaining per-block visibility flags rather than merging adjacent quads into larger primitives, and from [Blocky meshing](31-blocky-meshing.md) generally by focusing on incremental state updates rather than batch mesh generation.

### [Voxel Block Shape & Culling Configuration](2176-voxel-block-shape-culling-configuration.md)
A trait-based system that defines the geometry, transparency culling behavior, and lighting properties for individual block types within a voxel mesh generator. It solves the problem of heterogeneous block rendering by allowing each block ID to specify its own shape (e.g., cube, ramp, fluid) and how it interacts with neighbors during [face culling](#8735-face-culling.md). Unlike the parent method's generic solid/empty check, this configuration enables advanced culling modes such as merging shared faces between transparent blocks of the same type, and supports non-cube geometries like slopes and fluids.

### [Face Coverage Mask Culling](3397-face-coverage-mask-culling.md)
A method for optimizing blocky mesh generation by representing the geometric coverage of a voxel face as a bit mask, allowing for the culling of partially occluded faces from partial shapes (such as stairs and slabs). Unlike basic neighbor checks that treat faces as binary solid/empty, this method solves the problem where a boolean solid flag is insufficient because partial shapes have mixed visible and hidden areas on a single face. It sets itself apart from [Face Culling](8735-face-culling.md) by enabling fine-grained visibility decisions based on geometric overlap rather than simple adjacency, and from [Opacity-based Mesh Culling](8759-opacity-based-mesh-culling.md) by separating geometric coverage from material transparency properties.

### [ChunkMesh Vertex Packing and Management](3566-chunkmesh-vertex-packing-and-management.md)
A dynamic mesh generation and buffer management technique for voxel terrain, designed to minimize GPU memory overhead and draw calls by packing vertex attributes into compact integer formats and reusing vertex slots during incremental updates. It solves the problem of sparse, high-latency vertex buffer updates in blocky meshing by maintaining a free-list of unused vertex indices and uploading data via `DYNAMIC_DRAW` hints. Unlike static meshing approaches, it supports real-time addition and removal of blocks by logically remapping indices and notifying adjacent chunks of visibility changes.

### [Voxel Backface Culling and Internal Face Masking](4569-voxel-backface-culling-and-internal-face-masking.md)
This method optimizes [voxel mesh generation](#971-boolean-voxel-meshing.md) by rejecting invisible faces in projection space and masking faces shared between neighboring voxels. It distinguishes itself from standard neighbor-check culling by incorporating view-dependent backface culling directly into the geometry generation pipeline, ensuring that only front-facing, non-internal faces are emitted. It builds on [Face Culling and Visibility Optimization](3861-face-culling-and-visibility-optimization.md) by adding orientation checks relative to the camera.

### [Block Visibility Culling](5334-block-visibility-culling.md)
[Block Visibility Culling](#5334-block-visibility-culling.md) determines which voxel blocks require mesh updates or rendering based on the camera's position and rotation, avoiding unnecessary geometry generation when the view has not changed significantly. It operates at the coarse block level by comparing current camera coordinates and viewing direction against previous frame values, skipping index updates if both match. Unlike sibling methods that cull individual faces based on neighbor occupancy or surface orientation, this method optimizes the entire block's visibility state relative to camera movement.

### [Extraction of Surface Points (Sobierajski)](5721-extraction-of-surface-points-sobierajski.md)
[Extraction of Surface Points](#5721-extraction-of-surface-points-sobierajski.md) is a [direct volume rendering](#1184-direct-volume-rendering.md) method that accelerates surface visualization by extracting only the visible boundary voxels from the volume data. It solves the performance bottleneck of rendering entire isosurfaces by projecting a sparse set of surface points onto the image plane, ensuring coverage without generating a full mesh. It differs from sibling methods like [Voxel Block Placement with Face Culling](923-voxel-block-placement-with-face-culling.md) by operating in image space via projection rather than object space via geometry generation, and from [Face Culling and Visibility Optimization](3861-face-culling-and-visibility-optimization.md) by using viewing-direction-based visibility tests instead of neighbor-based internal face culling.

### [Mask Projection Culling](6836-mask-projection-culling.md)
[Mask Projection Culling](#6836-mask-projection-culling.md) is a visibility-based mesh filtering technique that removes faces and vertices not consistently observed across multiple camera poses by projecting 3D points into camera space and comparing their depth against rendered depth maps or binary masks. It differs from neighbor-based culling (e.g., [Face Culling](8735-face-culling.md)) by relying on external camera viewpoints rather than local voxel topology, making it suitable for sparse or non-voxelized meshes where occlusion from specific viewpoints must be resolved.

### [Mesh Culling via 3D Projection and Connected Components](6963-mesh-culling-via-3d-projection-and-connected-components.md)
This method removes invisible geometry and artifacts from a 3D mesh by projecting its vertices into multiple camera views and comparing their depths against reference depth maps. It distinguishes itself from neighbor-based culling (e.g., [Face Culling](8735-face-culling.md)) by operating on unbounded or complex meshes where voxel adjacency is not defined, relying instead on multi-view consistency to identify "seen" versus "unseen" regions. It serves as a post-processing step for [surface extraction](#29-surface-extraction.md) from radiance fields or point clouds, specifically targeting artifacts from unbounded [Gaussian splatting](#946-gaussian-splatting.md) reconstruction.

### [Face Culling](8735-face-culling.md)
Face Culling is a mesh generation optimization that prevents rendering block faces occluded by adjacent solid blocks, significantly reducing triangle count in homogeneous voxel terrain. It solves the problem of naively rendering all six faces of every cube, including those hidden by neighbors, by skipping the generation of internal faces. Unlike [Voxel Backface Culling and Internal Face Masking](4569-voxel-backface-culling-and-internal-face-masking.md) which operates during rasterization or [Block Visibility Culling](5334-block-visibility-culling.md) which operates at a higher level, Face Culling operates at the mesh construction phase to minimize the vertex/index buffer size sent to the GPU.

### [Opacity-based Mesh Culling](8759-opacity-based-mesh-culling.md)
[Opacity-based Mesh Culling](#8759-opacity-based-mesh-culling.md) is a post-processing technique applied to polygonal meshes derived from [neural radiance fields](#4972-neural-radiance-fields.md) or similar volumetric representations to reduce geometric complexity. It solves the problem of excessive triangle counts and low-opacity artifacts by removing faces that contribute negligible visual information. Unlike sibling methods that rely on spatial neighbor checks or block visibility [Face Culling and Visibility Optimization](3861-face-culling-and-visibility-optimization.md), this method evaluates the intrinsic opacity of individual mesh primitives. It sets itself apart by operating on the final extracted mesh geometry rather than the underlying voxel or splat data, directly filtering triangles based on their accumulated opacity values.

### [From-Region Visibility Preprocessing](9048-from-region-visibility-preprocessing.md)
[From-region visibility preprocessing](#9048-from-region-visibility-preprocessing.md) is a technique that precomputes which parts of a 3D scene are visible from specific regions of the camera space, allowing for the culling of occluded geometry during rendering. Unlike parent methods that rely on local voxel adjacency for face culling, this approach handles complex, non-axis-aligned geometry and large-scale datasets by determining visibility from a region rather than a single point. It is distinct from from-point approaches (e.g., [153]) which require little preprocessing but are limited to smaller, in-core datasets.

### Buried Bitmask Optimization
A bitmask used to track which blocks in a chunk are 'buried' (fully surrounded by opaque blocks), allowing the renderer to skip mesh generation for those blocks [S2, unofficial]. The algorithm resets the buried bitmask for the chunk, creates `MappedAdjacentChunks` for the current chunk position to access neighboring chunks, and iterates through all blocks in the chunk (0 to `CHUNK_SIZE`). For each block, it determines if it is buried by calling `block->isBuried(...)` and sets the corresponding flag in the bitmask. If all blocks in the chunk are buried (checked via `buriedBitmask->AreAllBlocksSet()`), the mesh is marked as empty and mesh generation is skipped. When generating the mesh, any block that is air or has its buried flag set in the bitmask is skipped [S2, unofficial].

### Two-pass transparent meshing with opaque separation
A meshing strategy that separates opaque and transparent geometry into two passes to ensure correct rendering order and reduce overdraw, by generating opaque faces between air/transparent blocks and transparent faces only for blocks touching air [S3, unofficial]. The first pass (opaque) generates faces for opaque blocks. If the chunk contains transparent blocks, it tests for opaque blocks (ignoring transparent and air), generating opaque faces between air and transparent blocks. Otherwise, it tests for non-air blocks. The second pass (transparent) tests for non-air blocks to mark only transparent blocks. It generates faces for all transparent blocks touching air but does not add faces between transparent and solid blocks (since solid blocks already have those faces). Solid block types are filtered out during the transparent pass by checking if the block type is transparent before constructing the AO value and adding it to the hashmap [S3, unofficial].

### Smart Leaf Rendering
A leaf block rendering strategy that preserves alpha cutouts on outer leaf surfaces while culling internal faces to reduce vertex count [S4, unofficial]. It is controlled by a global static enum `sLeafRenderMode`, which defaults to `ChunkRenderer::LeafRenderMode::Smart` [S4, unofficial].

### Hidden Face Extension
A proposed optimization where the 2D grid includes a 'don't care' state (2) to allow rectangles to extend into hidden areas, potentially reducing total rectangle count [S5, unofficial]. While this might reduce mesh size, it increases the load on the rasterizer [S5, unofficial].

## Background
The concept of removing interior polygons was introduced in the context of voxel-based procedural terrain generation, specifically for engines like Unity [S1, unofficial]. Early implementations used a brute-force approach of instantiating cube models, which was inefficient. To optimize, a class was added to reconstruct cubes from triangles and check for solid neighbors, rendering only the visible sides [S1, unofficial]. This reduced the number of triangles from 12 per cube (6 sides) to 2 per cube (1 side) for internal blocks [S1, unofficial]. The meshes were then combined into chunks to further optimize implementation, though this introduced engine-specific vertex limits (e.g., ~65,000 vertices per mesh in Unity) [S1, unofficial].
